transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-05-12 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alicia Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Huang (Redwood SE), Tom Reynolds (DataForge CTO), Priya Kapoor (Head of ML), Ethan Cole (SRE)

Summary: quick edge-cases demo focusing on long context handling, high TPS behavior, streaming backpressure and timeouts. Walk through of API, Console, and Redwood Optimize recommendations. Customer raised concerns about latency at scale, K V cache behavior, and private VPC egress. 

Topics: long context windows, streaming reliability & backpressure, timeout behavior, high TPS routing, cache warmup, quantized model variants, security (SOC2/KMS/VPC).

Transcript:
[00:00] Alicia: hi everyone thanks for joining, this is Alicia from Redwood, i have Marcus from our SE team, we'll do a ~45 minute demo and then leave time for q and a, sound good?
[00:08] Tom: yeah good to go, appreciate it Alicia. quick note we have a hard stop at 16:05 utc so hopefully fits.
[00:12] Alicia: noted, we'll prioritize the high TPS stuff. Marcus i'll hand over to you to kick off with the console and API flows.
[00:18] Marcus: yeah thanks Alicia, hey team, quick context — DataForge mentioned you have 2 primary concerns: very long context (100k token-ish docs in some analytics pipelines) and bursts of high TPS during nightly processes. i'll start with a console walkthrough, then an API demo showing streaming and backpressure handling, and finish with Optimize suggestions for batching and quantization.
[00:32] Priya: sounds good, the long context is the tricky bit. we currently chunk and re-rank but the windowing is painful and costs are spiking.
[00:38] Marcus: totally. so first the Console — i'll share my screen, you should see the project dashboard, model catalog, and a route config. (screen share noises)
[00:46] Alicia: (off-mic) while Marcus screenshares i'll call out that our demo uses a r edwood-llama-large-8q variant to show quantized perf, please ignore specific model names in this demo, we're demonstrating mechanics.
[00:58] Marcus: okay on screen, route config — you can pin a model, set batch windows, per-route timeout, fallback variants, and a streaming policy. i'll show a route called "df-longcontext" with sequence-length limit set to 120k, prefix caching turned on and kv-cache expiry at 72h.
[01:14] Ethan: kv-cache expiry at 72 hours, quick q — how does the cache behave when we restart pods in dedicated? do we lose priming?
[01:20] Marcus: good q. for Dedicated we persist prefix caches to local NVMe or an optional networked cache; restarts will attempt to warm from persisted snapshots — there's a potential cold start window. in Hosted we use warmed pools and continuous batching to mitigate that. (slight hesitation) apologies, sometimes the transcripts say "K V cache" or "KV cash" — that's our demo noise.
[01:35] Tom: got it. related: how do you route during a burst if our primary region is saturated? we need graceful fallbacks without breaking data residency.
[01:42] Alicia: we have smart routing policies — you can route by region/latency/cost and set policy-based fallbacks to a compatible model variant in the same region. if you need strict residency, we add a policy to avoid cross-region failover.
[01:52] Priya: ok but what about streaming — we've seen clients drop streams when proxy backpressure happens and our frontend times out at 30s. how does Redwood handle streaming backpressure?
[02:00] Marcus: good point. demo time — i'll call the streaming API with a large context and simulate a slow client.
[02:06] [02:06] Marcus: (typing sounds) here's a streaming call: POST /v1/streams with stream=true and chunk_size=2k tokens. on the server side we maintain a send buffer and backpressure signals; if the client stops consuming we respect TCP backpressure and can apply per-route send window limits then continue model progress while buffering up to configured bytes. if the buffer hits limit we'll trigger an adaptive shedding policy — we can pause generation or fall back to a compressed summary response.
[02:36] Priya: pause generation? that sounds risky for correctness.
[02:39] Marcus: yeah agree, it's a tradeoff — we prefer to preserve client integrity; by default we pause generation only for ephemeral bursts and resume when the client recovers. you can also set the route to always flush partial tokens so the client gets partial results rather than a big final.
[02:53] Tom: do you have metrics exposed? we need to alert on queued bytes and dropped chunks.
[02:58] Marcus: console has token-level metrics, queued bytes, latency percentiles per route, and streaming disconnect counts. you can hook that into our tracing or export via Prometheus.
[03:06] Ethan: when you said adaptive shedding, are you dropping tokens or switching to a lower-granularity output?
[03:10] Marcus: switching output types is an option — for example, we can switch to a structured summary call that uses much less tokens. dropping tokens only happens in extreme configured policies and is logged with audit trails.
[03:20] Priya: also timing out — our frontend enforces a 30s UX timeout. if Redwood takes longer because of long context compute, we need a model for streaming keep-alives or partial flushes.
[03:28] Marcus: we have keep-alives and heartbeat frames in the stream protocol. for long-context runs you can configure periodic partial flushes (every N tokens) so frontends get incremental updates and their timeout can be reset. we also support a callback webhook when the generation completes.
[03:40] Alicia: quick demo of timeouts — i'll flip to API playground and run a generation with 80k tokens prefix and small model to simulate compute.
[03:46] [03:46] Marcus: starting run... (some debugs) you can see the stream sending initial echo, then partials at intervals. note latency spikes around the 45s mark due to a simulated cache miss.
[04:02] Tom: that's what we see in prod — big cold starts cause 2-3x token latency. what are best practices to avoid that?
[04:09] Marcus: Optimize recommendations: pre-warm caches for critical paths, pin dedicated instances for peak windows, use prefix caching aggressively for repeated docs, and use quantized variants that reduce compute per token. Redwood Optimize produces per-route suggestions after analyzing traffic patterns — it will recommend batch sizes, quantization profiles, and caching TTLs.
[04:26] Priya: can Optimize give us concrete cost estimates for switching to 4-bit quantized models for our nightly job?
[04:31] Marcus: yes we can run a small eval on your sample prompts and produce a cost delta estimate and latency forecast. that's part of the POC.
[04:37] Ethan: on the POC — we will need to simulate 100k TPS bursts for 10-minute windows. do you support that load from Hosted or do we need Dedicated?
[04:45] Marcus: for 100k TPS it's typically Dedicated or a hybrid where we reserve Dedicated for peak windows and fall back to Hosted for overflow. we can show a cost model — Hosted with autoscaling can handle spikes but predictability and cold-start risk are better on Dedicated.
[04:58] Tom: what about circuit breakers and graceful degradation? we need to fail to a cheaper model that returns structured fallback instead of error.
[05:05] Marcus: yes that's a standard Redwood pattern: route-level failover to smaller variants + structured fallback responses. you can also configure automatic A/B rollouts and canary that will fail back to a stable model on error.
[05:15] Priya: any examples of high-tps customer setups?
[05:17] Alicia: we've done similar with a fintech customer — they used Dedicated reserved capacity for nightly scoring and a small Hosted pool for lower-latency interactive traffic. Marcus can share an anonymized benchmark.
[05:25] Marcus: i'll paste the benchmark link in chat after the call — it includes token/sec, latency p50/p95/p99 for quantized vs fp16.
[05:31] [05:31] (system noise)
[05:36] Tom: security — we need KMS, HSM support, SOC2 evidence, and SSO. is that supported for Dedicated/private?
[05:42] Alicia: yes. Private and Dedicated support customer-managed KMS, HSM integrations, SAML/SSO with SCIM user provisioning, audit logs exported to your SIEM, and SOC2 reports on request. for air-gapped we have an on-prem package.
[05:53] Priya: good. does the audit log include streaming partials or is it just request/response metadata?
[05:58] Marcus: audit logs capture request metadata and streaming session events; we can also log full payloads if required, but typically that's configured with retention/PII controls.
[06:08] Ethan: let's talk timeouts in- depth — if a model run goes beyond our frontend 30s, what's the recommended client pattern?
[06:14] Marcus: pattern: client opens stream, expects periodic partials; if a partial hasn't been received within N seconds, client shows progressive UI. for longer jobs use an async job API — submit job, poll or use webhook on completion. that way UX timeouts don't kill the server-side work.
[06:27] Tom: do you support chunked resumable uploads of context (eg large documents) so we don't re-send 100k tokens each request?
[06:33] Marcus: yes — we support storing large contexts as artifacts (blob store) and referencing them by id; the server then fetches or mounts them into runtime, combined with prefix caching to avoid reprocessing.
[06:40] Priya: nice. can we control who can access those artifacts?
[06:44] Marcus: RBAC on artifacts with role-based scoping and KMS encryption on stored blobs.
[06:49] [06:49] Tom: last question — how do you measure cost per 1k tokens with batching? our job does millions of tokens and batching can drastically change unit economics.
[06:56] Marcus: Redwood Optimize provides estimated units per batch, and we show per-route token-cost breakdowns in the Console. you can simulate different batch windows and see dev/test vs prod cost deltas. we'll run a simulation for your workload.
[07:06] Priya: can we do an extended POC that includes our nightly job and a streaming frontend? what's a typical evaluation plan?
[07:11] Alicia: typical plan: 2-week pilot — week 1: integration + security review, week 2: load-tests + Optimize tuning + cost report. after that we can move to a 90-day pilot on Dedicated if needed.
[07:20] Tom: we need to get legal and procurement involved — what's typical SLAs for Dedicated?
[07:24] Alicia: Dedicated has SLA tiers — 99.9% with priority support, enterprise tier includes SLOs on p95 latency. we'll share a SLA appendix in the procurement pack.
[07:32] Marcus: quick demo of streaming backpressure behavior — i'm going to throttle the client to 50ms reads per chunk. watch the queued bytes metric on the console.
[07:38] [07:38] Marcus: throttling now... you can see queued bytes rise to configured threshold then the route pauses generation and emits a "partial-compressed-summary" event.
[07:46] Priya: ok i see that in the console, the stream status shows "PAUSED -> RESUMED". there's a subtle log event "adaptive-shed: summary".
[07:54] Marcus: yes and it's tied to an alert rule you can enable.
[07:58] Ethan: edge case — what if a client disconnects permanently mid-run? do you keep output for retrieval or is it discarded?
[08:04] Marcus: configurable: default behavior is short-term retention (configurable TTL) so clients can reconnect with the session id and get buffered partial output; for sensitive data you can opt to not persist the payloads.
[08:16] Tom: performance numbers — can you summarize expected p95 for our 8k token typical response on quantized model vs fp16 at 1k TPS?
[08:24] Marcus: ballpark: quantized 8q model p95 ~ 120-160ms per token under sustained load on Dedicated; fp16 is ~200-280ms per token depending on hardware. but real numbers depend on batch sizes and sequence length — that's why Optimize runs the sim.
[08:39] Priya: ok that's helpful.
[08:41] Alicia: we have about 10 minutes left, do you want to dive deeper on any piece?
[08:45] Tom: can you quickly show the POC checklist and what artifacts you'll need from us?
[08:49] Marcus: yes — checklist: sample prompt set, infra diagram, target TPS profile, data residency constraints, security contacts. i'll paste that checklist in chat.
[08:58] Priya: one more thing — how do you handle model rollbacks mid-traffic? we've seen regressions before.
[09:02] Marcus: rollbacks are automated via the rollout engine: canary deploy 10% traffic, monitor evals against golden prompts, auto rollback on regression thresholds. also you can pin a route to last-known-good version.
[09:12] Tom: great. let's go to next steps then.
[09:15] Alicia: recap: Alicia to send pricing and SLA docs + quickstart; Marcus to run the 100k TPS benchmark and share spreadsheet; DataForge to send infra diagram and sample prompts. we'll schedule the private deep-dive. any other asks?
[09:28] Tom: please include the SOC2 and KMS/HSM integration notes in the packet.
[09:31] Alicia: will do. thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email.
